previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted with abdominal pain and fevers due to recurrent cholangitis in the setting of stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents. Imaging showed biliary duct dilation suggesting obstruction. He underwent ERCP which cleared a blocked stent, relieving the obstruction. He was treated for bacteremia with broad-spectrum antibiotics, later narrowed based on culture results, and for C. difficile infection with oral vancomycin. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic therapy. His condition improved with normalization of liver function tests and negative blood cultures. He was discharged home with a two-week course of IV cefepime and tigecycline, oral vancomycin, and instructions for drain care and follow-up.
problems: Malignant neoplasm of intrahepatic bile ducts
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)

biliary ductal dilatation. I think it is ok to do this without PO contrast
unless radiology protocols as needing it

obtained with intravenous contrast. Oral contrast was not administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were provided for review.

similar to ___. There is no pleural or pericardial effusion.

Evaluation of the intra-abdominal organs is limited by the markedly delayed
phase of intravenous contrast. Again seen is left hepatic lobe atrophy. 
Pneumobilia within the left intrahepatic ducts is similar to ___,
attesting to metallic CBD stent patency. Two metallic stents are seen within
the common bile duct extending from the duodenum into the right posterior and
left hepatic ducts. An internal external PTBD catheter courses centrally via
the left CBD stent and loops back on itself, unchanged. Intrahepatic bile

rather than the lumen of the gallbladder. The gallbladder is dilated with wall
thickening and pericholecystic stranding, concerning for acute cholecystitis. 
The gallbladder appears intact.

The spleen is enlarged to 15.9 cm, unchanged. Calcifications in the spleen
suggest prior exposure to granulomatous disease.  An adjacent accessory spleen
is noted. The pancreas and bilateral adrenal glands are normal.  There is no
hydronephrosis bilaterally.  An 11 mm simple cyst is seen in the left renal

The small and large bowel are normal in course and caliber without
obstruction.  A metallic density at the lesser curvature of the stomach
(05:25) is unchanged. There is no free intraperitoneal air. The abdominal
aorta is normal in caliber throughout without significant atherosclerotic
calcifications along its course.  Porta hepatic nodes, measuring up to 9-mm,
are unchanged since ___ (5:29).  No newly enlarged mesenteric or
retroperitoneal lymph nodes are identified.

CT PELVIS: The rectum is normal. Diverticula are seen in the sigmoid colon
without inflammatory changes. The bladder and prostate are unremarkable. There
is no free fluid and no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

BONE WINDOWS: No bone finding suspicious for infection or malignancy is seen.
Degenerative change is noted in the lumbar spine.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Percutaneous cholecystostomy tube has retracted, with pigtail coiled in
the abdominal wall. Dilated gallbladder with wall thickening and surrounding
stranding is concerning for acute cholecystitis.

2.  Unchanged position of biliary stents and internal-external biliary drain.
No intrahepatic fluid collection identified. No interval increase in biliary
duct dilation.

3.  Stable mild splenomegaly.

EXAMINATION:  PERCUTANEOUS CHOLECYSTOSTOMY TUBE PLACEMENT

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with h/o perforated gallbladder presents with
cholecystitis and fever and CT shows gallbladder drain came out of GB and is
in abdominal wall, needs replacement  // please reposition/replace GB drain

COMPARISON:  CT ___

PROCEDURE:  Ultrasound-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___, radiology fellow and Dr. ___,
attending radiologist, who was present and supervising throughout the total
procedure time.

TECHNIQUE:  The risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure were
explained to the patient.  After a detailed discussion, informed written
consent was obtained.  A pre-procedure timeout using three patient identifiers
was performed per ___ protocol.

The patient was placed in a supine position on the ultrasound table.

The existing percutaneous cholecystostomy tube was cut and removed.  The
existing site was deemed not adequate for access given limited visualization
of the liver by that approach. Limited preprocedure imaging was performed to
localize the gallbladder.  A new appropriate skin entry site was chosen and
the site marked.  Local anesthesia was administered with 1% Lidocaine
solution.

Using continuous sonographic guidance, an ___ drainage catheter
was advanced via trocar technique into the gallbladder.  A sample of fluid was
aspirated, confirming catheter position within the collection.  The metal
stiffener was removed. The pigtail was deployed.  The position of the pigtail
was confirmed within the collection via ultrasound.  Ultrasound images were
stored on PACS.

Approximately 10 cc of serosanguineous fluid was drained with a sample sent
for microbiology evaluation. The catheter was secured by a StatLock. The
catheter was attached to bag. Sterile dressing was applied.

The procedure was tolerated well, and there were no immediate post-procedural
complications.

SEDATION:  The patient received divided doses of 150 mcg fentanyl throughout
the total intra-service time of 35 minutes during which patient's hemodynamic
parameters were continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology
nurse.

FINDINGS: 

On real-time imaging prior to the procedure, the existing percutaneous
cholecystostomy tube with seen with a coil in the abdominal wall. The
gallbladder is dilated with wall edema.  Intra-procedure imaging demonstrates
the catheter coiled within the gallbladder.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful ultrasound-guided placement of ___ pigtail catheter into the
gallbladder. Samples was sent for microbiology evaluation.
